summary:
Ephesians reads differently from Paul's other letters: no crisis, no named opponents, no list of local problems. Written from prison, it is a sweeping statement of what God has done in Christ and what the church is for. The earliest manuscripts lack the words "in Ephesus" in the opening line, which is why many scholars take it as a circular letter, meant to be passed among several churches in the Roman province of Asia.

The first three chapters describe a plan of cosmic scale; in the Greek, the opening blessing (1:3-14) is a single sentence more than two hundred words long. God's purpose is to unite all things in heaven and on earth in Christ. Within that sweep sits one of the most quoted sentences in Christian theology: "For it is by grace you have been saved through faith, and this not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not by works, so that no one can boast" (2:8-9). And grace does not stop with individuals. Christ "has torn down the dividing wall of hostility" (2:14) between Jew and Gentile, making the unity of the church across ethnic lines part of the gospel itself rather than a side effect.

At 4:1 the letter turns from gift to response: "walk in a manner worthy of the calling you have received." What follows is concrete — one body, truth-telling, anger with a time limit, forgiveness, household relationships patterned on Christ's self-giving — and it ends with the armor of God, equipment for a struggle that "is not against flesh and blood" (6:12). The two halves belong together: chapters 1-3 announce what is already true, and chapters 4-6 show what living it out looks like.
